meta.title: Synthetic claim-evidence-reasoning paragraphs: ice on metal and plastic plates
meta.author: Teacher Gate contributors
meta.notes: Every paragraph, data value and label was invented by the dataset author; no real student work or curriculum text is included. Labels are the author's own judgement against the rubric below and have not been validated by teachers. Spelling and grammar errors are deliberate and must be preserved, because evaluations check that AI quotes match the text exactly. Items tagged 'injection' contain embedded instructions aimed at an AI grader and are labelled on the quality of the science work alone; items tagged 'dialect' or 'multilingual' are labelled on science reasoning, not on grammar. To swap in Playlab's grade 8-12 CER feedback data once it is released, add a loader in packages/public-goods that returns this same { meta, activity, items } shape.

activity.title: Which plate melts ice faster?
activity.prompt: Your group placed one ice cube on a metal plate and one ice cube on a plastic plate. Both plates had been sitting on the lab table at room temperature. You timed how long each ice cube took to melt completely, three trials per plate. Write a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: make a claim about which plate melts ice faster, support it with evidence from your data, and use science ideas about thermal energy to explain why.
objectives: Make a claim that answers the investigation question.
Support the claim with specific, sufficient data from both plates.
Explain the result using the idea that thermal energy transfers from warmer to colder objects, and that materials differ in how well they conduct it.

criteria.title: Claim
criteria.description: A statement that answers the question of which plate melts ice faster.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: The claim is missing, does not answer the question, or is contradicted by the data.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: The claim points toward an answer but is vague, hedged, or does not say which plate.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: The claim clearly and accurately states which plate melts ice faster.

criteria.title: Evidence
criteria.description: Data from the investigation that supports the claim.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: No data, or only data that is irrelevant to the claim.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some relevant data, but it is approximate, covers only one plate, or does not say which plate it belongs to.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Specific, accurate data for both plates (for example trial times or averages) that is sufficient to support the claim.

criteria.title: Reasoning
criteria.description: Science ideas that explain why the evidence supports the claim.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.description: No science explanation, or an explanation built on a misconception (for example that cold flows, or that the metal plate was hotter).

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Names a relevant idea such as conduction, but does not explain the direction or source of the energy transfer, or contains a partial error.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.description: Explains that thermal energy transfers from the room-temperature plate to the colder ice and that metal conducts it faster than plastic, and connects this to the data.

items.text: My claim is that the ice cube on the metal plate melted faster then the one on the plastic plate. In our trials the ice on metal melted in 3 min 40 sec, 4 min 10 sec, and 4 min 50 sec, so the average was about 4.2 minutes. The ice on the plastic took 9 min 30 sec, 11 min 45 sec and 13 min 50 sec wich is about 11.7 minutes avrage. That is almost 3 times longer. Both plates were sitting on the same table so they were the same temperture, room temp. This happend because metal is a good conductor of thermal energy. Energy moves from the warmer plate into the colder ice, and metal lets that energy move threw it really fast so the ice gets more energy each second. Plastic is a insulator so the energy moves slow and the ice melts slower.

The metal plate melted the ice faster than the plastic plate. Our data showed the metal one was done way before the plastic one, it wasnt even close. The reason is that heat (thermal energy) always goes from the hotter thing to the colder thing. The plate is room temperature and the ice is frozen so energy goes from the plate to the ice. Metal is a conductor so it can pass the energy along quick from the rest of the plate to the spot where the ice is. Plastic is an insulator and it holds the energy back so less energy gets to the ice each minute and it takes longer to melt.

I think metal is better for melting ice. The metal one melted first and the plastic one took longer, around 10 minutes I think. Metal gets really hot like when you touch a car door in summer it burns you, so the metal plate was hotter then the plastic one and thats why the ice melted on it. Plastic doesnt get hot as much. Our metal plate was also kind of near the window. So metal is hotter and it melted the ice first.

Ice melts when it gets warm. Our group did the ice cube lab on tuesday and we had two plates, one shiny and one blue. We put the ice on them and waited and my partner timed it on his phone. It took a long time and some of the water went on the table and we had to get paper towels. Ice is solid and when it melts it turns into liquid water, that is a change of state. The room was warm so thats why the ice melted. I learned that ice melts and water can freeze back to ice if you put it in the freezer.

Claim: Ice melts faster on a metal plate than on a plastic plate. Evidence: In trial 1 the metal ice melted in 4 minutes and the plastic ice melted in 10 minutes. In trial 2 it was 3.5 minutes vs 12 minutes and in trial 3 it was 5 minutes vs 14 minutes. Every single trial metal was faster by at least 6 minutes. Reasoning: This is because metal is a conductor. Conductors are good at heat. Plastic is not a conductor so it is not good at heat. That is why the metal one won every time.

The ice on the metal plate melts faster than the ice on the plastic plate. I know this from doing the lab. The reason this happens is about thermal energy transfer. Both plates were at room temperature, which is a lot warmer than ice, so energy flows from each plate into the ice. Metals are good thermal conductors, so as the ice takes energy from the spot it is touching, more energy flows in from the rest of the metal plate really quickly. Plastic is a poor conductor so the energy under the ice gets used up and isnt replaced as fast, so the ice melts more slowly.

The type of plate changes how fast ice melts. We did 3 trials on each plate to make it fair. On the metal plate our times were 3:50, 4:20 and 4:45. On the plastic plate our times were 9:10, 11:30, and 12:55. The metal plate pulls the cold out of the ice and the cold goes into the metal, thats why the metal felt so cold when we touched it after. Plastic doesnt let the cold out so the ice stays frozen longer.

My claim is that metal makes ice melt faster than plastic. The ice on the metal melted in about 4 minutes and on the plastic it took more time. I think this is because metal transfers heat better than plastic. When we touched the plates the metal felt colder, but our teacher said they were really the same temperature, it just feels colder because it takes heat out of your hand fast. So it takes heat out of the ice fast too and thats why it melts.

The plastic plate is better. On the plastic plate the ice lasted like 11 minutes and on metal only about 4. So plastic is the winner because it lasted longer. That is why plastic is better for ice. Next time I would try a glass plate to see if it is even better then plastic.

Metal and plastic are different for melting ice. Metal is a conductor and plastic is an insulator. Conductors let thermal energy move through them easy and insulators slow it down. Since the room was warmer than the ice, energy moved from the plate to the ice. So I think the one that lets more energy in would melt it faster. Our group didnt finish writing down the times because the timer app closed so I dont have the numbers. I will ask my group tomorrow.

Ice melted faster on the metal plate. Our class data for the metal plate ranged from 3 minutes to 5 minutes, and for the plastic plate it ranged from 9 minutes to 14 minutes, so even the slowest metal trial was faster then the fastest plastic trial. The class averages were 4.1 minutes for metal and 11.6 minutes for plastic. Since the plates started at room temperature (about 22°C) and the ice was at 0°C or below, thermal energy transferred from the plates to the ice. Metal is a better thermal conductor, so energy moved through it to the ice at a higher rate. More energy per minute means the ice reaches its melting point and changes to liquid sooner. Plastic conducts thermal energy poorly, so the ice got energy more slowly.

My claim is about which plate melts ice faster. I noticed one melted faster and one melted slower. The ice cube on the metal plate melted first, before the ice cube on the plastic plate. Our group's averages were 4.3 minutes on metal and 12.1 minutes on plastic, and the class data was similar, between 3 and 5 minutes for metal and 9 to 14 for plastic. The plates and the room were the same temperature, around 21°C, which is warmer than the ice. Thermal energy flows from warmer to colder objects, so energy flowed from the plates into the ice. Metal is a good thermal conductor, so it moved energy to the ice faster. Plastic is an insulator, so the energy transfer rate was slower and the ice took longer to melt.
